**Quinces, Late Light**

A dark still life on a worn table: a green-black bottle standing at the back left, a warm bowl holding two quinces, two more fallen on the table, and a folded linen running off the right edge. Everything is built on a narrow range of earths — raw and burnt umber, ochre, lead white, a little ultramarine and green earth — with cadmium yellow and transparent oxide yellow carrying the only bright note in the picture.

The light rakes in from the upper left and does almost all the work: it catches the bottle's left edge and shoulder, runs along the bowl's rim, turns each quince from a lit cream to a warm brown core, and falls away to the right where the cloth and the far table go into shadow. The wall sits around 0.18 and the table around 0.22, so the quinces read as the picture's one light event.

Working honestly, the cloth is the weak passage — it holds its shape but never quite stopped reading as a pale slab rather than linen — and the table still carries a raised, cobblestone relief from a glaze I laid too lean, which I only partly flattened. The forms are also more plainly drawn than I first wanted: the fruit are cleanly turned but a little bald, and the bowl's wall stayed soft. Squinting, though, the value structure holds, which is the test that matters most.

**Title: *Quinces, Green Bottle, Low Light***

The picture is a low-key still life on a warm brown table against a dark wall. A dark green-black glass bottle stands at the back left; a wide, shallow dark bowl sits centre, holding two quinces; two more lie loose on the table in front of it. Light enters from the upper left and dies out across the picture, so the right-hand side of the table and the whole upper wall sink into shadow. The four quinces are the only light notes in the picture — olive-gold, downy, each with a small stem dimple — and everything else is kept dark so they read as the subject.

It began three days ago with a folded linen at the right, which I painted out: I could not make it read as cloth rather than a pale slab, and it was wrecking that side of the canvas. Letting the right fall away into shadow made the whole picture stronger, and I spent the rest of the work rebuilding the quinces (they had gone bald and faceted with hard yellow caps), turning the bowl from a pale lens into a dark glazed vessel, and calming the wall and table into flat, quiet fields with a proper fall of light across them.

Two things I'd flag honestly. First, my journal for this session is mostly a record of damage: I ghosted the quinces three times by blending a table mask that touched them, painted a wall glaze over the tops of the fruit because `wallm` runs behind the bowl, and lost the whole picture to one bad unifying glaze that laid pale curls over everything and had to be rebuilt. Second, the surfaces are too smooth — I modelled and blended almost everywhere, so the picture is quieter and more airbrushed than Tonn's broken, stroke-driven handling. The quinces are the only passage with real brush character in them.

**Four Quinces**

The picture is a low-key still life on a warm brown ground: a black-green glass bottle standing at the back left, a wide dark glazed bowl with two quinces nestled in it, two more quinces lying on the table, and the light coming in from the upper left and dying away across the right-hand side. The quinces are the only light note in the picture — everything else, bottle, bowl, wall, table, falls away into a narrow range of umbers and browns, with the bottle's silhouette the one hard dark shape against the wall.

I spent this session rebuilding it from the ground up: the wall and table were re-laid as clean fields, the bowl was remodelled with a lit rim along its front left, the bottle was knocked back to a dark silhouette with a single grey reflection running down its left side, the fruit were repainted from scratch, and the cast shadows were re-cut so everything sits on the table. Squinting, the value structure holds — a dark band across the top, the lit table through the middle, four small bright notes sitting in it.

It is, honestly, over-smoothed: almost everything is a blended gradient rather than broken brushwork, and I spent too long chasing soft modellings when I should have been leaving the strokes alone. The one thing I did learn properly is that the only reliable way to build a soft form on a small object here is to lay the modelling blotchily and then blend it inside the mask; every other route to a gradient — `load_at`, clip gradients, stipple, soft-edged masks — streaks, blotches or speckles.

**Quinces, Raking Light**

A low-key still life: a dark green-black glass bottle at the back left, a wide dark glazed bowl holding two quinces, and two more quinces on a warm brown table, the light coming in from the upper left and dying away into shadow at the right. The four quinces are the only light note in the picture — mottled olive-gold with dark speckling and a dry calyx at the crown — and the two in the bowl sit a step darker than the two in front so the bowl reads further back. The bowl itself is almost pure black: it is drawn by a single bright warm line along its near lip, which crosses in front of the fruit, and a thin edge light down its front-left; the bottle is held together by a green-grey turn, two broken white glints and a warm bounce off the table.

What I know is still not right, and would be the first thing I attack with another day: the wall and the table are grained but even, and Tonn's fields are built of visible standing strokes — mine are laid down and smoothed — and the fruit mottling runs a shade too close to camouflage in close-up.
